background.definition: Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma (NHL) is a heterogeneous group of lymphoproliferative malignancies arising from lymphocytes with differing patterns of behavior and responses to treatment. NHLs are grouped as either aggressive or indolent lymphoma (also known as "low-grade lymphoma"; see ).

list.listitem: Estimated 81,000 new cases and 20,600 deaths from NHL in the Unites States in 2021 (American Cancer Society statistics).
International incidence varies, with highest rates in the United States, Europe, and Australia; incidence has increased by 4% annually. The lowest rates are seen in Asia.
U.S. estimated prevalence was 743,000 people living with non-Hodgkin lymphoma in 2018 (SEER statistics).
In a cost analysis, mean monthly costs were $5871 for aggressive NHL and $3833 for indolent NHL.
For aggressive NHL, mean monthly initial treatment phase costs ($10,970) and palliative care costs ($9836) were higher than costs incurred during secondary phase ($3302).
The mean cost of treatment failure in aggressive NHL was $14,174 per month and $85,934 over the study period.
NHL is the fifth leading cause of cancer death and the second fastest growing cancer in terms of mortality.
Approximately 2% of men and women born today will be diagnosed with NHL at some time during their lives.
The median age at diagnosis was 67 years. Approximately 95% of cases occur in adults 40 to 70 years of age, and men are more often affected than women.
The exact cause of NHL is not known.

A variety of risk factors has been identified (see ), but most patients with NHL have no known risk factors. Increased intake of fruits and vegetables is associated with a modestly reduced risk of NHL.
Studies have shown little relationship between exposure to cigarette smoke or to ionizing radiation and the risk of NHL. Adult survivors of childhood cancer are at greater risk, though.
A retrospective cohort study found no association between inflammatory bowel disease and the risk of developing lymphoma.
A systematic review of four studies with 1,188 cases of ocular adnexal lymphoma has demonstrated a significant association between chlamydia infection and MALT histotype of this low grade lymphoma.
In low grade salivary gland MALT lymphoma there is an association with Sjogrens syndrome in almost 30% patients.
NHL begins when a lymphocyte (a B cell or T cell) becomes abnormal. About 85% of NHLs occur in B cells.

Four main mechanisms of pathogenesis are recognized: (1) accumulation of gene alterations in the tumor genome; (2) infection of the tumor clone by an oncogenic virus; (3) stimulation and selection of tumor cells by an antigen; and (4) immunodeficiency of the host.
Although the precise role of these mechanisms varies, clonal accumulation of genetic lesions is a prerequisite in the pathogenesis of all subtypes of NHLs.

list.listitem: Take a complete history for involvement of major organs, extranodal sites, and B symptoms. C
Examine the lymph node areas, the liver and spleen, the Waldeyer's ring, and the testes. C
Open biopsy of enlarged lymph nodes is mandatory for diagnosis. B

For the staging, or extent of the disease, a complete blood work-up, blood chemistry, erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), LDH, and CT scan of the neck, chest, pelvis, and abdomen should be performed. B
Imaging with PET-CT for initial staging and for subsequent assessment of response is now standard of care in aggressive NHL.

Differential.Differential_Name: Infections: infectious mononucleosis, cat-scratch disease, and cytomegalovirus infection
Differential.Differential_Features: Patients should be evaluated for infectious processes, and lymph node biopsy should be performed
Absence of Reed-Sternberg cells is characteristic for NHL
Extensive nodal involvement, fewer circulating abnormal cells, fewer blast forms in the marrow are considered for NHL

Differential.Differential_Name: Auto immune diseases: Sjogren's syndrome, systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), rheumatoid arthritis (RA)
Differential.Differential_Features: Order serologic tests (antinuclear antibody, rheumatoid factor, etc.); lymph node biopsy should be done; patients should be closely observed

Differential.Differential_Name: Rare lymphoproliferative diseases: Castelman's disease, sinus histiocytosis
Differential.Differential_Features: Castelman's disease often present with a localized lymph node. Atypical histocytes in lymph nodes are characteristic for sinus histiocytosis

list.listitem: The Ann Arbor staging system is commonly used for patients with NHL.
"B" symptoms are: unexplained loss of more than 10% of body weight in the 6 months before diagnosis, unexplained fever with temperatures above 38°C, drenching night sweats.

For those without such symptoms, Stage I: Involvement of a single lymph node region (I) or localized involvement of a single extra lymphatic organ or site (IE). Stage II: Involvement of two or more lymph node regions on the same side of the diaphragm (II) or localized involvement of a single associated extra lymphatic organ or site and its regional lymph nodes with or without other lymph node regions on the same side of the diaphragm [IIE; note: the number of lymph node regions involved maybe indicated by a subscript (e.g., II3)]. Stage III: Involvement of lymph node regions on both sides of the diaphragm (III) that may also be accompanied by localized involvement of an extralymphatic organ or site(IIIE), by involvement of the spleen (IIIS) or both (IIIS+E). Stage IV: Disseminated (multifocal) involvement of one or more extra lymphatic sites with or without associated lymph node involvement or isolated extralymphatic organ involvement with distant (nonregional) nodal involvement.

The most common symptom of NHL is painless enlargement of lymph nodes, anywhere in the body. In a retrospective study, NHL was the second most common cause (35%) of malignant peripheral lymphadenopathies in children. Most frequent presentation is in the neck. In that study, in either the generalized or the localized LAP group, the cervical region was the most common area (30.3% and 85%, respectively).
Systemic symptoms ("B symptoms") include unexplained fevers, drenching night sweats, and weight loss and are seen in about 10% of patients with NHL.
Other symptoms may include an enlarged liver or spleen, chest pain, shortness of breath, or generalized fatigue.
15% to 20% of NHLs occur in lymphoid tissue elsewhere in the body. The gastrointestinal system is the most common primary extranodal site.
Determine risk for HIV infection, previous history of immune disorder or treatment with immunosuppressive drugs, use of hair dyes, and family history of lymphoma.

If NHL is suspected, initial testing should include open biopsy of enlarged lymph nodes. Fine-needle aspiration biopsy (FNA) is not desirable for the initial diagnosis. Histologic grading cannot be performed on an FNA.

Staging should include: CBC, LDH, chemistries including renal and hepatic function, ESR, hepatitis B testing, serum beta-2-microglobulin, bone morrow biopsy, uric acid, chest x-ray, and CT or MRI scan of the chest, pelvis and abdomen.
Additional useful tests are PET scan (preferred) or gallium-67 scan and serum protein electrophoresis.

Serum beta-2-microglobulin is a protein found on the surface of white blood cells. Increased production or destruction of these cells causes beta-2-microglobulin levels to increase in cancer patients. Elevated beta-2-microglobulin level was found to be a negative prognostic factor for overall survival.
CT scan can help to determine whether any lymph nodes or organs in the abdomen, pelvis, chest, head, and neck are enlarged.

Bone marrow biopsy can be used for determining the malignant cells in bone marrow for staging of NHL. Bone marrow involvement rates were reported to be between 11% and 33% in aggressive NHL and between 40% and 70% in low-grade NHL.
Imaging with PET-CT scan may be more sensitive and specific than CT for assessing response after chemotherapy in patients with aggressive NHL and is now standard of care for these patients.
Suspect NHL in any patient presenting with painless lymph node enlargement or fevers, chills, and weight loss ("B symptoms").
Perform a complete history and physical exam of any lymph node chains, the liver and spleen, the Waldeyer's ring, and the testes.

Open biopsy of enlarged lymph nodes is mandatory. If the biopsy reveals NHL, the next step is staging with a complete blood work-up, blood chemistry, ESR, LDH, chest X-ray, and CT or MRI scan of the chest, pelvis, and abdomen.
Chemotherapy is the main treatment modality for both indolent and aggressive NHL. A

Early-stage indolent NHL: For asymptomatic patients, no treatment is needed. Radiotherapy may be used with potentially curative intent for some patients with stage I/II disease. Chemotherapy with radiation therapy and rituximab either alone or in combination with chemotherapy are other treatment choices. B

Advanced-stage indolent NHL: For asymptomatic patients, no treatment is needed. For symptomatic patients, the recommended initial treatment is R-CVP (rituximab, cyclophosphamide, vincristine, prednisone). Radiotherapy can be used for individual sites of disease with palliative intent. B
Early-stage aggressive NHL: Treat with short course (typically 3-4 cycles) multi drug chemotherapy plus rituximab, with involved-field radiotherapy. B

Advanced-stage aggressive NHL: Treat with combination chemotherapy for a longer duration than is used for early-stage disease (typically 6 cycles); combining the CHOP regime with rituximab (monoclonal antibody) improves the results. Radiotherapy may be used for residual disease or for previously bulk disease at the end of chemotherapy, to reduce the risk of relapse. B
Surgery is occasionally performed to remove an organ (such as the spleen) or part of an organ that is badly damaged by a lymphoma.
Because of recent improvements in imaging, exploratory surgery is rarely used to classify NHL.
There is no clinical evidence to suggest that alternative therapies are effective in treating NHL.

In general, chemotherapy is the main treatment modality for both indolent and aggressive NHL. Specific treatment chosen depends on whether the tumor is indolent or aggressive, and can be guided by the Revised International Prognostic Index for patients with diffuse B-cell lymphoma (). Treatment options include chemotherapy, monoclonal antibody therapy, radiation therapy, watch and wait, bone marrow transplantation, surgery, experimental treatments, symptom management.

Early-stage indolent NHL: For asymptomatic patients, no treatment may be given initially. Radiotherapy alone may be used with potentially curative intent for some patients. Chemotherapy with radiation therapy and rituximab (a specific monoclonal antibody directed against a specific molecule called CD-20 on the surface of normal and malignant B lymphocytes) either alone or in combination with chemotherapy are other treatment choices. A Cochrane review of 5 RCTs with 1245 patients found that adding radiotherapy to chemo therapy improves survival in patients with early stage NHL.

Advanced-stage indolent NHL: For asymptomatic patients, no treatment is needed initially. For symptomatic patients, the recommended initial treatment is R-CVP (rituximab, cyclophosphamide, vincristine, prednisone). A combination of cyclophosphamide, vincristine, and prednisolone was less effective than R-CVP in a Phase 3 RCT. Radiotherapy can be used for individual sites of disease with palliative intent. A recent RCT of the bendamustine-rituximab combination demonstrated longer progression free survival and less toxicity than RCHOP in patients with indolent NHL.

Early-stage aggressive NHL: Treat with several courses of multidrug chemotherapy (usually CHOP) plus rituximab, with involved-field radiotherapy. A Cochrane review did not find benefit of high dose chemotherapy with stem cell transplantation over standard chemotherapy in patients with aggressive NHL.

Advanced-stage aggressive NHL: Treat with combination chemotherapy for a longer duration than is used for early-stage disease (typically 6 cycles); combining the CHOP regime with the monoclonal antibody rituximab improves the results. Radiotherapy may be used for residual disease or for previously bulk disease at the end of chemotherapy, to reduce the risk of relapse. A randomized trial with 1080 patients found no difference between 14 and 21 day cycles, so 21 day cycles are preferred.

Peripheral T cell lymphoma: a trial showed improved progression free and overall survival with the addition of brentuximab vedotin to cyclophosphamide, adriamycin and prednisolone over CHOP chemotherapy alone.

A trial randomized 879 previously untreated patients with intermediate or high risk diffuse large b-cell lymphoma to R-CHOP (rituximab, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, and prednisone) or to a modified regimen that replaced vincristine with polatuzumab vedotin. Patients in the pol-R-CHP group were more likely to experience progression free survival (77% vs 70%, p = 0.02) but with no difference in overall survival.
In patients with high IPI scores (assessment of risk) a systematic review has shown no benefit for autologous transplant in first remission.

A non-controlled prospective cohort study identified 154 patients with relapsed or refractory DLBCL. They were pretreated with obinutuzumab followed by 12 cycles of glofitamab monotherapy. The median time to complete response was 42 days, and 78% maintained that response at 12 months. Grade 3 or worse adverse events occurred in 62%, though.
A randomized trial found that patients given levofloxacin 500 mg daily on the 7 days post R-CHOP chemotherapy had fewer episodes of fever and febrile neutropenia.

Chimeric antigen receptor T-cell therapy (CAR-T) is a recent development in B cell malignancies which have proven refractory to standard treatments. This is a very expensive therapy with high risks of toxicity (eg cytokine release syndrome) but the early response rates are promising in a challenging group of patients.

Randomised trials of CAR-T therapy using axicabtagene ciloleucel as second-line treatment for early relapsed or refractory diffuse large B cell lymphoma (DLBCL) have shown mixed results. For the axi-cel agent, a trial of over 300 patients comparing against standard of care in second line (salvage chemotherapy plus a transplant) demonstrated higher response rate (83% vs 50%) and higher event free survival at 2 years with axi-cel therapy (41% vs 16%).
On further follow-up this same trial confirmed a higher overall survival rate at 4 years follow-up of 54% versus 46% with standard of care.

In contrast a study with the alternative CAR-T agent tisagenlecleucel randomising 322 patients between CAR-T and standard of care showed similar response rates in both arms (46% versus 43%) and a higher incidence of progressive disease at 6 weeks in the CAR-T arm.

For follicular lymphoma, adding interferon alfa-2b was found in a systematic review of 8 RCTs to improve progression free survival, although the effect on overall survival is less clear. In an RCT of induction treatment for patients with follicular lymphoma, those randomized to obinotuzumab-based chemotherapy had higher rates of progression free survival (80% vs 73%) and lower mortality than those randomized to rituximab based therapy. However, serious adverse events were more common with obinotuzumab (46% vs 39%).

An RCT compared rituximab plus chemothearpy with rituximab plus lenalidomide in 1030 patients with previously untreated follicular lymphoma. Complete response at 120 weeks and progression free survival were not significantly different between the groups. More patients in the rituximab + chemotherapy group had moderate or severe neutropenia (50% vs 32%), more febrile neutropenia (7% vs 2%) and more skin reactions (7% vs 1%). Thus, rituximab + lenalidomide appears to be similarly effective but better tolerated.

Mantle cell lymphoma is apparently indolent in morphology, but is associated with worse outcomes than other 'low-grade' NHL. Standard of care in young patients is now defined as immunochemotherapy followed by stem cell transplant. Addition of cytarabine in younger patients pre transplant is associated with improved outcome. There is a benefit to rituximab after transplant in younger patients with mantle cell lymphoma.

A clinical trial randomized 523 patients 65 and older with untreated mantle-cell lymphoma to ibrutinib 560 mg orally once daily until disease progressed or the drug was not tolerated or placebo; all patients received six cycles of bendamustine 90 mg/m2 body-surface area and rituximab 375 mg/m2. At a median 85 months follow-up, progression free survival was higher with ibrutinib (HR 0.75 for progression; 95% CI 0.59 to 0.96) but not overall survival. Complete response was numerically more likely with ibrutinib as well (65.5% vs 57.6%, p = 0.06).
A Cochrane review found no RCTs evaluating the effectiveness of stem cell transplantation for patients with advanced primary cutaneous T-cell lymphoma.

Burkitt lymphoma is characterised by very rapid proliferation but is chemosensitive with more aggressive chemotherapy than standard CHOP. It is a B cell NHL, so also benefits from addition of rituximab.
NICE guidelines suggest that pixantrone, a topoisomerase II inhibitor, can be effective in multiply relapsed NHL.
Varicella vaccine reduces the risk of herpes zoster in patients with hematologic malignancy (RR 0.54).

The exact combination of drugs and how long they are given depend on the type of NHL. A typical course of chemotherapy involves six to eight cycles, given every 3 weeks, for total treatment duration of 18 to 24 weeks.
Dosages of radiation usually range from 25 G to 40 G over 3 to 4 weeks.
Hospitalization is or may be needed for patients undergoing higher dose chemotherapy, stem cell/bone marrow transplantation, radiation therapy plus chemotherapy programs, comorbidities.
Hospitalization may also be needed for severe emesis, life-threatening infections, severe pain, or nutritional support.
Pelvic irradiation and large cumulative doses of cyclophosphamide have a high risk of permanent sterility.
Antibiotic prophylaxis in afebrile neutropenic patients on chemotherapy has been demonstrated to reduce all cause mortality.

For up to 2 decades after diagnosis, patients are at significantly elevated risk of second primary cancers, especially lung, brain, kidney, and bladder cancers and melanoma, Hodgkin's disease, and acute nonlymphocytic leukemia.
Left ventricular dysfunction is a significant late effect of long-term survivors of high-grade NHL who received more than 200 milligrams per meter squared of doxorubicin.

A systematic review and meta-analysis of risk of cardiac events in patients treated for haematological malignancies confirms the elevated risk. For treated patients compared to control population the hazard ratio for developing acute myocardial infarct is 1.65, for heart failure is 4.82 and for stroke is 1.60.

A randomised placebo-controlled trial examining the effect of atorvastatin in patients receiving anthracycline chemotherapy demonstrated a reduced incidence of cardiac dysfunction following chemotherapy in those who received atorvastatin for 12 months, which merits further consideration.
Myelodysplastic syndrome and acute myelogenous leukemia are late complications of myeloablative therapy with autologous bone marrow or peripheral blood stem cell support.
Indolent NHL types have relative good prognosis, with median survival as long as 10 years, but the aggressive type of NHL has a worse prognosis. C
The 5-year survival rate for those diagnosed at age 15 to 44 years is 65%, whereas for those aged 65 to 74 years it is 37% and those aged 85+ years 13%. B
Nomograms for overall and cancer-specific 3, 5 and 8 year survival have been developed. B
Low-grade NHL typically remains asymptomatic for years (indolent) and in the elderly has little impact on life expectancy.
Indolent NHL is usually diagnosed at a late stage; some 70% of patients will have bone marrow involvement at the time of diagnosis.
High-grade NHLs are aggressive and can be rapidly fatal diseases.
NHL does not have a clear pattern of spread from one area to the next, and dissemination is often wide and unpredictable, with frequent lung and hepatic involvement.
Indolent NHL has a relatively good prognosis, with a median survival as long as 10 years, but usually it is not curable in advanced stages. The aggressive type of NHL has a worse prognosis.
The 5-year survival rate for those diagnosed at ages 15 to 44 years is 65%; for those aged 65 to 74 years it is 37% and those aged 85+ years 13%.
In general, with modern treatment of NHL patients, overall survival at 5 years is approximately 50% to 60%. Among patients with aggressive NHL, 30% to 60% can be cured.
shows a clinical decision rule to predict the outcome for patients with NHL.
Nomograms for overall and cancer-specific 3, 5 and 8 year survival have been developed.
Prognosis is not affected by socioeconomic status.

Most relapses occur in the first 2 years after therapy. Visits should be every 3 months for 2 years, then every 6 months for 3 years, then annually. Assess response 1 to 2 months after completion of therapy.
After complete remission, no special investigation is needed beyond physical examination and CXR if the patient is asymptomatic.
Patients with partial remission should be regularly monitored with CT scanning and blood tests at 3-month intervals for at least 18 months for relapse of the disease.
The risk of NHL rises with age. Age >60 years and especially age >70 years are associated with worse prognosis.
For older patients with asymptomatic advanced-stage low-grade NHL, a watch-and-wait policy is recommended. The optimal management of very elderly patients (age >80 years) has not been defined.

For patients with aggressive lymphoma, age alone should not be a contraindication for treatment, and probably adequate therapy should be administered with the highest dose that the patient can tolerate. Comprehensive geriatric assessment can contribute usefully to treatment planning in the elderly population with diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBL).
Most NHL are aggressive in pregnancy, and delay of therapy until after delivery appears to have a poor outcome. Thus, immediate therapy can be considered.

There are no data regarding long-term effects on children exposed inutero for most of the chemotherapeutic agents. Abortion in the first trimester may be an option that allows therapy for women with aggressive NHL.
Early delivery when feasible may minimize or avoid exposure to chemotherapy or radiation therapy.
Treatment may be delayed for those women with an indolent NHL.
NHL in children is generally considered to be widely disseminated from the outset, even when apparently localized.
Combination chemotherapy is recommended for most patients.

There are two potentially life-threatening clinical situations: (1) superior vena cava syndrome (or mediastinal tumor with airway obstruction), most often seen in lymphoblastic lymphoma, and (2) tumor lysis syndrome, most often seen in lymphoblastic and Burkitt or Burkitt-like NHL.
Children with limited disease have an excellent prognosis when treated with chemotherapy.
Radiation is not used as front line therapy for children but can play an ancillary role as emergency treatment for the above-mentioned complications.
For children treated in more recent decades, the risk of second malignancies following therapy is lower with the reduction in chemotherapy and radiation doses.
